lesson.title: Microcontrollers: sense, decide, act
lesson.subtitle: The tiny computer inside every smart device, and the loop it runs

video.title: Microcontrollers: sense, decide, act
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: A light that knows it's dark
Start with or without a kit

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor in a dim school corridor holding a small board with an LED and a light sensor; the LED glows.
scenes.animation: The corridor darkens; the LED fades on by itself.
scenes.narration: Our corridor is dark by five, and someone always forgets the light. My pupils built a light that switches itself on. A light sensor, an LED and a tiny computer, smaller than a bank card. Let me show you what's inside.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: microcontrollers, the tiny computers that sense, decide and act.

scenes.visual: A chip zooms open to show a processor and memory, with pins around the edge. Then a washing machine, a charger and a meter, each with the same chip glowing inside.
scenes.animation: Zoom into the chip; then three appliances pop in.
scenes.on_screen_text: A whole computer on one chip
scenes.narration: A microcontroller is a whole small computer on one chip: a processor, memory, and pins that connect to the world. It's inside washing machines, phone chargers, prepaid meters and weather stations. Boards like the Arduino, the micro:bit and the ESP32 make them easy to use in class.

scenes.visual: A board in the middle; on the left, a button, a light sensor and a thermometer wire in; on the right, an LED, a buzzer and a small motor wire out.
scenes.animation: Left items slide in, then right items.
scenes.narration: Its pins are inputs and outputs. Inputs bring news in: a button, a light sensor, a thermometer. Outputs act: an LED, a buzzer, or a motor through a driver. Analog input pins turn a voltage into a number.

scenes.visual: A circle of four arrows: read, decide, act, wait, spinning; a small box labelled setup sits before it.
scenes.animation: Setup ticks once; the circle starts spinning.
scenes.narration: The program has two parts. Setup runs once, when the power comes on. Then the loop runs again and again, many times a second: read, decide, act, wait. That loop is the heart of every smart device.

scenes.visual: The four steps of the loop fill in with the night light's details, beside a sensor reading going up and down.
scenes.animation: Each step writes in as it is said; the LED switches on when the reading dips below 300.
scenes.narration: Here's the night light. Read the light sensor: more light gives a bigger number, from zero to one thousand and twenty-three. Decide: below three hundred means dark. Act: switch the LED on, or else off. Wait a tenth of a second, and go round again.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor points at a reading of 800 on a small screen; the LED is hidden behind a card. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! The sensor reads eight hundred, and our rule says dark is below three hundred. Is the LED on or off?

scenes.visual: The card lifts: the LED is off; the reading 800 sits far above a line at 300.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; the loop arrow ticks round once.
scenes.narration: Off. Eight hundred is well above three hundred, so it's bright. The loop will check again in a tenth of a second.

scenes.visual: Three tables: a board with LEDs; a phone showing a simulated micro:bit; a pupil holding a program card in front of the class.
scenes.animation: Each table slides in as it is named.
scenes.narration: There are three ways to start. With a board: an Arduino or a micro:bit, a few LEDs and a light sensor. With a phone or a computer: free simulators like MakeCode and Wokwi run in a browser. And with nothing at all: one pupil plays the microcontroller and follows a program card.

scenes.visual: A smooth wave becomes dots, then a staircase; sliders for 'how often' and 'bits' move.
scenes.animation: The staircase gets finer as the bits slider rises.
scenes.on_screen_text: In the lab: signals to numbers
scenes.narration: In the lab, you'll see how a microcontroller turns a smooth signal into numbers. Choose how often it measures, and how many bits it uses, and watch what's lost.

scenes.visual: Amina in the corridor at noon under a grey sky; the LED is on. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.on_screen_text: On at noon: what to change?
scenes.narration: Your turn. On cloudy days our corridor is dim, and the night light switches on at noon. What should we change?

scenes.visual: The rule's number slides from 300 to 200. Then four icons line up: sensor, rule, LED, loop.
scenes.animation: Icons line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Lower the number in the rule, say to two hundred: then it only counts as dark when it's really dark. Remember: a microcontroller reads its inputs, decides with a rule, acts on its outputs, and loops. Change the rule, and you change the device.

scenes.visual: A pupil at the front holds a program card and a torch, glancing at the window; classmates cover the window with a book and she switches the torch on.
scenes.animation: The window darkens; the torch clicks on.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: one pupil is the microcontroller. Give her a program card: look at the window, decide with the rule, and switch a torch on or off. Then, if you can, build the same night light in a simulator.

checkpoints.prompt: The sensor reads 800, and the rule says dark is below 300. Is the LED on or off?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — 800 is well above 300, so it's bright and the LED stays off.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — more light gives a bigger number. 800 is far above 300, so it's bright: the LED is off.

checkpoints.prompt: On cloudy days the night light switches on at noon. What should we change?

options.text: Lower the number in the rule

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — with a lower number, only a really dark corridor counts as dark.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a faster loop makes the same decision more often. The rule's number decides what counts as dark.
